newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices soar to 27-month high, supplies scarce.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices soar to 27-month high, supplies scarce.

text.p: Coffee prices staged an explosive rally Tuesday as scarce supply propelled the market to its highest level in 27 months.
"You just don't have a plentiful supply of coffee right now," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka, noting there may be scope for prices to climb further.
"What the market will do now is correct in the next day or two, then maybe go up again," Spilka said. "I don't see stocks increasing."

The market came within striking distance of the widely watched 200 cents ($2) a lb mark, hitting a session high of 199.50 cents on May futures on the New York Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange before the benchmark contract closed up 10.40 cents at 195.25 cents.
Coffee prices last traded above $2 in 1994 when two severe frosts in top-grower Brazil led to sharply depleted world supply.
Frozen concentrated orange juice futures also rose sharply, boosted partly by the prospect of a strike in the key Brazilian port of Paranagua.

Paranagua port operators said Tuesday they had failed to reach an agreement with dock workers at the key Brazil port and confirmed a 72-hour strike would begin at noon local time (1500 GMT) Wednesday.
"The strike has been confirmed. It is scheduled for tomorrow at midday until Saturday at midday," said Carlos Roberto Frisoli, vice president of the port operators union SINDOP.
The strike will affect cargoes of wood orange juice and cotton, which rely on manual labour.
A port authority spokeswoman said shipments of Brazilian soybeans, soymeal and corn from Paranagua will be unaffected because they are automated.
The benchmark May orange juice contract on the New York Cotton Exchange settled 5.90 cents higher at 87.70 cents a lb.
Some analysts, however, remained bearish on the outlook for orange juice with Florida expected to produce a record 220 million 90-lb boxes in the 1996-97 crop year.
NYMEX crude oil futures ended higher after staging a late rally on short covering and technical strength ahead of weekly oil inventory data.

"We were able to hold the (technical support) numbers today and that's what took us up. But fundamentally nothing has changed," said Michael Busby, trader with Northville Industries in Melville, New York.

April crude settled up 41 cents at $20.66 a barrel. Oil prices have lost more than 20 percent in the last month due to refiners cutting crude usage to make seasonal repairs while mild winter temperatures have slackened heating oil demand.
April gasoline ended up 1.12 cents a gallon at 62.89 cents and April heating oil finished 0.16 cent higher at 53.34 cents.
